## Introduction

The `pcmt` package provides permutation-calibrated variants of conditional
independence tests from the `comets` package. The key trade-off:

- **Asymptotic tests** (`comets::gcm`, `comets::pcm`): fast (one regression fit),
  but rely on CLT-based calibration that may be inaccurate in finite samples.
- **Permutation tests** (`pcmt::perm_gcm`, `pcmt::perm_pcm`): require $B + 1$
  regression fits, but achieve exact validity under the strong exchangeable null
  while maintaining asymptotic validity under the weaker conditional null.

This vignette benchmarks the speed difference and shows how closely the two
approaches agree in terms of p-values and calibration.

**A note on the PCM comparison.** `comets::pcm` includes a variance estimation
step (`est_vhat = TRUE` by default) that divides the direction function by an
estimated conditional variance. `perm_pcm` omits this step (it uses the
vanilla PCM direction). To make the test statistics comparable, we pass
`est_vhat = FALSE` to `comets::pcm` throughout. Similarly, `comets::pcm`
internally applies a `sign(rho)` correction so that the statistic is positive
under the alternative, effectively making it a one-sided test. We match this
by using `alternative = "greater"` in `perm_pcm`.

## Setup

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(pcmt)
library(comets)
library(ggplot2)
```

We use a simple linear DGP throughout. Under the **null**, $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z$:

$$
Z \sim N(0,1), \quad X = Z + \varepsilon_X, \quad Y = Z + \varepsilon_Y
$$

where $\varepsilon_X, \varepsilon_Y \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)$,
so $X$ and $Y$ are correlated marginally but conditionally independent given $Z$.

```{r dgp}
generate_data <- function(n, effect = 0) {
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(n), ncol = 1)
  X <- Z + rnorm(n)
  Y <- Z + effect * X + rnorm(n)
  list(Y = Y, X = X, Z = Z)
}
```

## Speed Comparison — GCM

We compare wall-clock time for the asymptotic GCM (`comets::gcm`) against
the permutation-calibrated GCM (`pcmt::perm_gcm`) with varying numbers of
permutations $B$.

```{r speed-gcm}
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
dat <- generate_data(n)
B_vals <- c(99, 199, 499)
n_rep <- 5  # average over a few runs

time_asymp <- system.time(
  for (i in seq_len(n_rep))
    comets::gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z, reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm")
)[["elapsed"]] / n_rep

time_perm <- vapply(B_vals, function(B) {
  system.time(
    for (i in seq_len(n_rep))
      pcmt::perm_gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z,
                     reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm", B = B)
  )[["elapsed"]] / n_rep
}, numeric(1))

gcm_timing <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Asymptotic (comets)", paste0("Permutation (B=", B_vals, ")")),
  Time_sec = round(c(time_asymp, time_perm), 4)
)
knitr::kable(gcm_timing, col.names = c("Method", "Time (sec)"),
             caption = "GCM timing with linear regression (n = 200)")
```

## Speed Comparison — PCM

The PCM involves more regressions per permutation (direction estimation +
projection refit), so the cost per permutation is higher.

```{r speed-pcm}
set.seed(2)
n <- 200
X3 <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), ncol = 3)
Y_pcm <- X3[, 2] + X3[, 3] + rnorm(n)  # Y indep X1 | X2, X3

time_asymp_pcm <- system.time(
  for (i in seq_len(n_rep))
    comets::pcm(Y_pcm, X = X3[, 1, drop = FALSE], Z = X3[, -1, drop = FALSE],
                reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                est_vhat = FALSE)
)[["elapsed"]] / n_rep

time_perm_pcm <- vapply(B_vals, function(B) {
  system.time(
    for (i in seq_len(n_rep))
      pcmt::perm_pcm(Y_pcm, X3, target = 1,
                     reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                     reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                     B = B, alternative = "greater")
  )[["elapsed"]] / n_rep
}, numeric(1))

pcm_timing <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Asymptotic (comets)", paste0("Permutation (B=", B_vals, ")")),
  Time_sec = round(c(time_asymp_pcm, time_perm_pcm), 4)
)
knitr::kable(pcm_timing, col.names = c("Method", "Time (sec)"),
             caption = "PCM timing with linear regression (n = 200)")
```

## P-value Agreement Under the Null

We generate many datasets under the null and compare asymptotic vs
permutation p-values. With linear regression and a linear DGP, both
approaches should agree closely.

```{r pval-null}
set.seed(42)
n_mc <- 200
B <- 199

pvals_null <- data.frame(
  gcm_asymp = numeric(n_mc), gcm_perm = numeric(n_mc),
  pcm_asymp = numeric(n_mc), pcm_perm = numeric(n_mc)
)

for (i in seq_len(n_mc)) {
  ## GCM null: X indep Y | Z
  dat <- generate_data(n = 200, effect = 0)
  g_a <- comets::gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z,
                     reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm",
                     alternative = "greater")
  g_p <- pcmt::perm_gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z,
                         reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm",
                         B = B, alternative = "greater")
  pvals_null$gcm_asymp[i] <- g_a$p.value
  pvals_null$gcm_perm[i]  <- g_p$p.value

  ## PCM null: Y indep X1 | X2, X3
  X3 <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 3), ncol = 3)
  Y_pcm <- X3[, 2] + X3[, 3] + rnorm(200)
  idx <- sample.int(200, 100)
  p_a <- comets::pcm(Y_pcm, X = X3[, 1, drop = FALSE],
                     Z = X3[, -1, drop = FALSE],
                     reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                     reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                     est_vhat = FALSE, indices = idx)
  p_p <- pcmt::perm_pcm(Y_pcm, X3, target = 1,
                         reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                         reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                         B = B, indices = idx,
                         alternative = "greater")
  pvals_null$pcm_asymp[i] <- p_a$p.value
  pvals_null$pcm_perm[i]  <- p_p$p.value
}
```

```{r scatter-null, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot(pvals_null$gcm_asymp, pvals_null$gcm_perm,
     xlab = "Asymptotic p-value", ylab = "Permutation p-value",
     main = "GCM — Null", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.4))
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(pvals_null$pcm_asymp, pvals_null$pcm_perm,
     xlab = "Asymptotic p-value", ylab = "Permutation p-value",
     main = "PCM — Null", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.4))
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Under the null with a well-specified linear model, the asymptotic
approximation is accurate and both p-values fall close to the diagonal.

## P-value Agreement Under the Alternative

Under a clear alternative ($X \to Y \mid Z$), both tests reject. We check
how their p-values compare.

```{r pval-alt}
set.seed(123)

pvals_alt <- data.frame(
  gcm_asymp = numeric(n_mc), gcm_perm = numeric(n_mc),
  pcm_asymp = numeric(n_mc), pcm_perm = numeric(n_mc)
)

for (i in seq_len(n_mc)) {
  ## GCM alternative: Y = Z + 0.5*X + eps
  dat <- generate_data(n = 200, effect = 0.5)
  g_a <- comets::gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z,
                     reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm",
                     alternative = "greater")
  g_p <- pcmt::perm_gcm(dat$Y, dat$X, dat$Z,
                         reg_YonZ = "lrm", reg_XonZ = "lrm",
                         B = B, alternative = "greater")
  pvals_alt$gcm_asymp[i] <- g_a$p.value
  pvals_alt$gcm_perm[i]  <- g_p$p.value

  ## PCM alternative: Y = X1 + X2 + X3 + eps (X1 has effect)
  X3 <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 3), ncol = 3)
  Y_pcm <- 0.5 * X3[, 1] + X3[, 2] + X3[, 3] + rnorm(200)
  idx <- sample.int(200, 100)
  p_a <- comets::pcm(Y_pcm, X = X3[, 1, drop = FALSE],
                     Z = X3[, -1, drop = FALSE],
                     reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                     reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                     est_vhat = FALSE, indices = idx)
  p_p <- pcmt::perm_pcm(Y_pcm, X3, target = 1,
                         reg_YonXZ = "lrm", reg_YonZ = "lrm",
                         reg_YhatonZ = "lrm", reg_RonZ = "lrm",
                         B = B, indices = idx,
                         alternative = "greater")
  pvals_alt$pcm_asymp[i] <- p_a$p.value
  pvals_alt$pcm_perm[i]  <- p_p$p.value
}
```

```{r scatter-alt, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot(pvals_alt$gcm_asymp, pvals_alt$gcm_perm,
     xlab = "Asymptotic p-value", ylab = "Permutation p-value",
     main = "GCM — Alternative", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.4))
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(pvals_alt$pcm_asymp, pvals_alt$pcm_perm,
     xlab = "Asymptotic p-value", ylab = "Permutation p-value",
     main = "PCM — Alternative", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.4))
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

## P-value Calibration (QQ Plots)

Under the null, p-values should be uniformly distributed. We plot QQ plots
of the null p-values against `Uniform(0, 1)`.

```{r qq-plots, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
qq_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    p = sort(pvals_null$gcm_asymp),
    Method = "Asymptotic", Test = "GCM"
  ),
  data.frame(
    p = sort(pvals_null$gcm_perm),
    Method = "Permutation", Test = "GCM"
  ),
  data.frame(
    p = sort(pvals_null$pcm_asymp),
    Method = "Asymptotic", Test = "PCM"
  ),
  data.frame(
    p = sort(pvals_null$pcm_perm),
    Method = "Permutation", Test = "PCM"
  )
)
qq_data$theoretical <- rep(ppoints(n_mc), 4)

ggplot(qq_data, aes(x = theoretical, y = p, colour = Method)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Test) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles (Uniform)",
       y = "Observed p-value quantiles",
       title = "QQ plot of null p-values") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Both methods track the diagonal closely, confirming proper calibration under
the null with a well-specified linear model.

## Summary Table

```{r summary-table}
alpha <- 0.05

summary_df <- data.frame(
  Test = c("GCM", "GCM", "PCM", "PCM"),
  Method = rep(c("Asymptotic", "Permutation"), 2),
  `Median time (sec)` = round(c(
    gcm_timing$Time_sec[1],
    gcm_timing$Time_sec[3],  # B = 199
    pcm_timing$Time_sec[1],
    pcm_timing$Time_sec[3]   # B = 199
  ), 4),
  `Type I error` = c(
    mean(pvals_null$gcm_asymp <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_null$gcm_perm <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_null$pcm_asymp <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_null$pcm_perm <= alpha)
  ),
  Power = c(
    mean(pvals_alt$gcm_asymp <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_alt$gcm_perm <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_alt$pcm_asymp <= alpha),
    mean(pvals_alt$pcm_perm <= alpha)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(summary_df,
             caption = "Summary: n = 200, B = 199, linear regression, 200 MC reps")
```

The permutation tests are slower by a factor of roughly $B + 1$ regressions,
but they achieve comparable type I error control and power in this
well-specified setting. The permutation approach becomes especially
valuable when the asymptotic approximation is unreliable (e.g., small $n$,
heavy tails, or complex nonlinear regression).
